messages.subject: Two questions re multivariate GWAS
parts:
Hi Andrew, Eliot, and Michel,

Hope this finds you doing well and enjoying your summer (at least as best you can, given the current circumstances). I had 2 quick questions for you. We have been conducting a multivariate GWAS on the four higher-order Psychopathology factors that we found in our structural analyses described in our forthcoming World Psychiatry paper (see biorxiv #https://doi.org/10.1101/502039). One of the things we’d like to report along with the other analyses is the percent of the genetic correlations among the four Psychopathology factors accounted for by all of the SNPs. Can we get this by using the genetic correlations that could be reported in the measurement model output for the mvgwas and comparing those to the genetic correlations that are reported in the output for the measurement model alone, that is without doing the mvgwas? And is it possible to get such output for the measurement model in the overall mvgwas, rather than the measurement model for each SNP? Second, in conducting post-GWAS analyses of each factor (e.g., gene-based tests) we need to specify the N for the GWAS for each factor. Would it be more appropriate to use the overall N for the mvgwas, given that the 4 factors are correlated, or the overall summed N for the constituent GWASs for each factor?

Thanks!
Irwin

messages.author: 0b5254eeb9973d7a
messages.subject: Re: Two questions re multivariate GWAS
parts:
Hi Irwin,

Please see my thoughts below.

All the best,

Elliot
One of the things we’d like to report along with the other analyses is the percent of the genetic correlations among the four Psychopathology factors accounted for by all of the SNPs.

I'm not sure what you mean here. The LDSC estimates of genetic covariance among phenotyeps (or the genetic correlations among latent factors estimated from a no-SNP model) are indeed the genetic correlations accounted for by all of the SNPs. If you are interested in the extent to which the model produces expectations that are consistent with the unmodelled LDSC strucuture, you can you standar LISREL matrix algebra, or path tracing rules, to produce the expected covariances and plot them against the LDSC-estiamted covariances. We do an example of this in the Appendix of the de la Fuente paper (https://doi.org/10.1101/766600).

If alternatively you are interested in the residual covariance between factors after accounting for a linear combination of the (noisy) betas from all SNPs, you'd need to do something like residualize the genetic covariance matrix for the expectation of a polygenic score derived from the sumstats from your multivariate model. I haven't worked that math out, but I would recommend against it for the very same reason that you don't want test what proportion of SNP h2 is accounted for by a PGS effect estimated in the same data in which the sumstats to produce the PGS were derived.

Can we get this by using the genetic correlations that could be reported in the measurement model output for the mvgwas and comparing those to the genetic correlations that are reported in the output for the measurement model alone, that is without doing the mvgwas?
And is it possible to get such output for the measurement model in the overall mvgwas, rather than the measurement model for each SNP?

The parameter estimates from "measurement model" that you specify are estimated separately for each SNP (in which case there is no "overall" set of estimates, apart from those obtained from the no-SNP model), unless you have fixed them in advance.

Second, in conducting post-GWAS analyses of each factor (e.g., gene-based tests) we need to specify the N for the GWAS for each factor. Would it be more appropriate to use the overall N for the mvgwas, given that the 4 factors are correlated, or the overall summed N for the constituent GWASs for each factor?

I would recommend that you consider using the effective N formula (separately for each set of sumstats for each factor) that Mallard et al. specify in their supplement (https://doi.org/10.1101/603134). Be careful, as this formula could produce non-sensible estimates for traits with low polygenicity, or when low powered GWASs are used.

Thanks!
Irwin
